Chapter 7: Final Illness—Surrender, Compassion, and the Mystery of Suffering.
As the body grew weaker, the world seemed to shrink. Suddenly, the everyday routines of the convent—climbing stairs, finishing small tasks, even just catching your breath—became real challenges.
Illness used to feel like something that happened to others, maybe far off in the future. But now, it was shaping every single day. Doctors came and went, there were hushed conversations in the hallway, and you could sense the gentle concern of sisters doing their best to ease the pain.
The future, always a little uncertain, now seemed to narrow down to one question: how do you live well, even when you’re suffering?
Most of us, when faced with illness, want to fight back. We hang on to our independence, to our strength. But here, a different path began to unfold. Every new limitation—every moment you had to ask for help—became an invitation to let go, to surrender. It was a chance to set aside pride and that instinct to do everything yourself.
The ‘Little Way’—which might have meant doing small things with great love—suddenly took on an even deeper meaning. Now, it wasn’t about what you could do, but how you could simply be. It wasn’t about achievement; it was about acceptance. A simple smile for a nurse, a quiet word of thanks, or enduring discomfort without complaint—these became powerful ways to show love, even when you felt weakest.
And something else happened: compassion deepened.
The pain of illness opened the heart to the suffering of others—people nearby, and even those you’d never meet. Suddenly, there was this real sense of kinship with anyone who struggled. You might find yourself wanting to carry their burdens, holding them in your prayers. Letters arrived from people looking for comfort, or maybe just some gentle advice, and each one was answered with honesty and warmth.
Of course, it was tempting to turn inward, to focus only on your own pain. But there was a choice to reach out—to give, even from a place of weakness. And that brought a surprising kind of joy.
One afternoon, as sunlight drifted through the window, she listened to the convent’s quiet—the laughter of novices far away, soft footsteps in the hall. The world outside kept turning, indifferent to her pain. But in that small room, something mysterious was happening: suffering, embraced with love, became a source of life for others.
It wasn’t just a personal trial anymore—it became a way to join in something bigger, to offer pain for the good of the world.
The final illness wasn’t a story of defeat. It was about transformation.
The body grew weaker, sure—but the heart? It only grew stronger. The ‘Little Way’ became a path through the deepest valleys, a reminder that, even in the darkest moments, it’s still possible to love.
Most people are afraid of losing control when illness comes. But here, surrender opened the door to peace.
